utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We just have one procedural matter that we wanted to raise before calling the witness, and it requires us to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The Prosecution calls another witness, Vlado Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated, Mr. Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, are you able to follow me in the language you understand?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Vlado Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I am going to go through your background information just -- and just ask you if you could confirm it. You were born on the 1st of August, 1961, in Saborsko. You graduated from secondary school in Ogulin in 1981. You served your military service between 1982 and 1983. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: After that, you worked at the National Park at Plitvice Lakes. You were there until the end of 1989, and at the end of 1990 you joined police. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You lived in Saborsko at -- at the time you joined police. Can you just briefly tell us something about Saborsko. How many households were in Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In Saborsko there were about 300 households, about 300 family houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And how many inhabitants, approximately?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: About 800 or 850, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to refer you again to the atlas, Exhibit 23. On page 20, grid A4, you can see Saborsko; however, this time I would like to refer you to the previous page, page 19, because you will have a better picture of the whole area. And on the page 19, you would see Saborsko in grid D3, and in this square you -- Saborsko is in the top right corner.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Before you joined police, you work at the National Park at Plitvice. Why did you leave your job at the national park?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: To put it quite simply, it's quite evident why I left my job in the national park in 1989. The epicentre of the evil started in Pakrac in 1991. The war started in Lipice park in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: But you left in 1989, so what made you leave at the end of 1989?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: There were negative rumours going round. It started in 1987. There was some kind of congress. Yugoslavia fell apart, and euphoria emerged in the National Park of Plitvice. Some of us, a group of us, four, saw that we were unwanted there. We had worked together all over the former Yugoslavia, but now we were unwanted, so we left.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said "us four." What nationality are you and those three who left at the end of 1989 the Plitvice area?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The three of us were Croats, and one was a Serb. And there was one Bosniak who remained, he was a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This Plitvice area, which ethnicity -- inhabitants of which ethnicity prevail in this area? And I am referring to 1989/1990.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: At Plitvice there was a majority of Serbs. I don't know how many there were, but I know most people were Serbs and the rest of us were in the minority. In the hotels, the staff -- well, everybody knew that, the hotel staff and the people working in the companies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Later, at the end of 1990, you joined police. Why did you join police?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I joined the police, quite simply, because new times had come. The Republic of Croatia had been created. This was a time of democracy, and I joined the police because in 1985, when I finished my primary school, I was not considered suitable to be a policeman in the former Yugoslavia, although I was best in gym classes. What was important at the time, in communist times, was for you to be politically suitable, not for you to be able. I did not succeed. I had good marks in school, and I was the best in Zagreb in my gym classes, but I was told I hadn't passed. When the Croatian state was created, then I was able to join the police, and I am still a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you still remember when exactly you joined the police?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The 15th of December, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you take any initial course?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were sent for training right away. There was symposia, seminars, about the law on the police, the criminal code, the law on traffic safety, the law on misdemeanours. And in the meantime, I was a policeman on the beat and guarding various facilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What was your assignment after the training?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Beat duty and patrol duty. And also for a while we guarded crucial facilities. For example, railway stations, various buildings, power-plants, and so on in the Republic of Croatia; everything that needed to be secured.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Where were you assigned? Which police station, in which town?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It was the police station in Ogulin. That's the former municipality of Ogulin which had a police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Ogulin?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I stayed in Ogulin until the 1st of April, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And where did you go after 1st of April?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: We were transferred to Saborsko, where there was a police outpost, because what happened on the 1st of April, 1991, meant that on the very next day a police outpost was established in Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, what was it what happened on the 1st of April?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of April -- you mean at Plitvice or --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said that what happened on the 1st of April, 1991, meant that on the next day a police outpost was established in Saborsko. So there was something which made you to move to Saborsko or made that the police station was established in Saborsko. What was it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for the simple reason that at Plitvice there was the first armed clash. The National Park of Plitvice and Saborsko are right next to each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So you left for Saborsko after 1st of April. Who left for Saborsko; which policemen?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Twenty employees, and on the 2nd of April we established the outpost from the police station of Ogulin.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Those who left for Saborsko, were they of Croat ethnicity or also Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The employees who lived and worked there were Croats, but our superiors from Ogulin who issued the orders to us, the second-ranking man in the Ogulin police station, was a Serb by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you also aware of the situation at Plaski police station at the time?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew about that situation. That was a Plaski police outpost which was set up in 1990 before the Saborsko police outpost. I knew about the situation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what was the situation in Plaski. Who worked there and did anybody leave from Plaski police station after 1st of April?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The people who worked in Plaski police outpost were policemen of the Croatian police who were both Croats and Serbs. I wasn't there, but in March the Croatian policemen who were Croats left the Plaski police station, during March, as far as I know, but I didn't work there myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you were already in Saborsko, did any of these Plaski policemen came to Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They came to Plaski and Ogulin. Some went to work in Ogulin and some went to work in Saborsko with us, those policemen of the Ministry of the Interior who were of Croat ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When they arrived to Saborsko, did you learn from them what made them to leave Plaski?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. They were supposed to sign some kind of confirmation. They couldn't explain it well. There was one in the shift who said that you had to sign that you would work for the Republic of Srpska Krajina. That was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you by any chance learn who asked them to -- to sign this confirmation or declaration?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The declarations -- well, rallies were organised, allegedly, for people to sign. Who it was who arrived from Knin, I don't know, but I do know that people resisted and that there were policemen of Serb ethnicity working for the Ministry of Interior of Croatia who didn't want to sign. But those who were there would know better than me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You also mentioned that there were some rallies organised. Who organised these rallies?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was the local leaders who wanted to create the Republic of Srpska Krajina. Now we hear that they were local leaders in Plaski, and who it was that came from Knin or other parts of the so-called Republika Srpska Krajina, I don't know that. Who organised a rally in Plasko, well I know that now because I've been talking to people in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So what did you learn? Who organised it at that time? What did you learn now?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In my conversations with people over coffee, we talk openly about the events that happened at that time. It was the local people in Plasko who called themselves - I don't know what - Martic's men. It's not clear to me. Those were the local leaders. Later, when I was captured, I saw what this was all about.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Okay. We will talk about your -- the time when you were captured later. Now, let's return to Saborsko. So after these policemen from Ogulin and Plaski arrive in Saborsko, how many of them were they altogether?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: There were 20 of us in Saborsko. Twenty more or less; maybe 22, 18. We weren't always in full strength.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were there any reserve policemen?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, later, ten reserve policemen were mobilised, about ten, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What kinds of weapons did you have?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: We active-duty policemen had long and short barrels, that means a pistol 76.2 millimetres, and a rifle, Zastava rifles, 7.9 millimetres. The reserve policemen only had long barrels.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What were your duties in Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1991 or --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm referring to 1991, from April onwards.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I was the operative duty officer, the chief of the shift.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What did you do? Did you set up any check-points? What kind of work did you do, you, all policemen?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It was patrol and beat duty, and we did have check-points, yes, in Borik, Kuselj, and towards Plitvice. Those were check-points.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were there any military facilities in the region? I'm not talking exactly about Saborsko, but the whole region.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The closest military facility was the Licka Jasenica railway station where there was a JNA barracks. It was not under our authority. We could not approach it. There were large fuel depots there. This belonged to the JNA and the Republika Srpska Krajina right until Operation Storm in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were JNA soldiers or JNA vehicles passing Saborsko from April when you were in Saborsko? Did you see any vehicles or soldiers passing through Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Every day JNA armoured vehicles passed through. They went along the Korenica-Josipdol road, the D42 road: Korenica, Plitvice, Saborsko, Plaski, Josipdol, two JNA armoured vehicles together.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did they have to go through your check-points?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you cause any -- did you block them from -- did you try to block them from passing through your village?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. We were even under orders not provoke them and to have no contact with them whatsoever. They simply passed by. They were armoured vehicles, and we only had rifles, so what could we do to them? And the command was that the -- the orders we had were not to have anything to do with them and not to provoke them at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said that they were passing every day. Do you still remember until when they were able to pass through your village or until when they were passing through your village?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They passed through as a sort of buffer zone with, that's what they said about themselves, until the 5th of August, 1991, when the first open attack began with 82-millimetre shells on Saborsko. So this went on right until the 5th of August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What about Plaski, was it a -- was it cut off by -- the road to Plaski, was it cut off by Croats or were you able to -- were Serbs able to go by the road?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The road to Plaski -- well, traffic was supposed to go along the Plaski-Plitvice-Josipdol road, but in Plaski and Licka Jasenica, the road was closed off - that was the information we heard - and this was done by various groups in Plaski. As for us, as far as we were concerned, the road was open.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what about Ogulin, were you able to travel to Ogulin?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was -- there was a line between Ogulin and Saborsko on a daily basis, a bus line, and the bus went every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you know or did you heard from anybody whether these buses could -- could go through Licka Jasenica without any problems or were they stopped?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They were stopped every day and searched in Plaski or in Licka Jasenica. We were always in contact with that bus driver. He was the only driver who was a Serb. He was the only one who was able to drive that bus, and he was the one who told us that the bus was stopped every time and the passengers searched.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you learn who searched the bus and -- did they search only the bus or also the people on the bus?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They searched both the bus and the passengers on the bus. The bus driver always reported to us about what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And because I combined two questions in one sentence, who did the searches?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, according to the bus driver, it was Martic's groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now I would like to focus on events of 5th of August. You said that it was the first time you were openly attacked. Can you tell me, where were you on 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 5th of August I was on duty that night as the duty officer, and we had a report by telephone that we should look out because we were going to be attacked. Somebody from Plaski or Licka Jasenica called us to warn us about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know, who was it who warned you?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Citizens in Licka Jasenica. We still talk about it today. Everybody knows who these people were. They were people who wished us well, and they told us: Look out, you're going to be attacked. And this was during the night, but we were not attacked until 6.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did they also tell you who is going to attack you?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. They just said: Watch out, you're going to be shelled. I was the one who received the report. Those were mortar shells.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So when the shelling started?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: My shift ended at 0600 hours on the 5th of August, 1991, and I remember it well because the first shell landed about five minutes after my shift ended. Then it was followed by another one, and then the attack escalated and went on until 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Which direction the shelling was coming from?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The shells were coming from Licka Jasenica and a hamlet there called --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the name of the hamlet, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the name of the hamlet.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Vukelic Poljana. It's a hamlet of the village of Licka Jasenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Maybe we didn't mention it at the beginning. Which -- inhabitants of which ethnicity live in the village of Licka Jasenica?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Inhabitants of Licka Jasenica were 100 per cent Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you able to conclude who shelled you?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Those were, in fact, mortar shells, 82 millimetres, issued by the JNA. And it's well-known who it is; it's the JNA and the local leaders, so-called Martic's men.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: At that time of the shelling, apart from you regular policemen from Saborsko, were there any other armed forces in the village of Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had 20 men sent to us at reinforcement from Duga Resa.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Preceding the attack on Saborsko, were there any ultimatums or demands made from any side?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, there were no demands made.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: During the 5th of August, was there any damage done to the buildings?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 5th of August, around 80 shells fell before 10.00 a.m., that is, between 6.00 a.m. and 10 a.m., and there was no material damage.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you able to see whether they -- they targeted something specifically?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: We couldn't understand whether they were not aiming right or what, but they were shooting to the right of the church. Maybe their target was the church, but the shells hit, in the morning, the area to the right of the church. However, in the evening, shells began falling in the centre of the place.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What about the civilian population of Saborsko? Did they -- on 5th of August, did they stay in the village or did they leave?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They left Saborsko, for the most part on the 6th, that is the night of the 5th, and they went to Rakovica. Not everybody but most everybody left.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And did they stay in Rakovica or was there any time when they would return back?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The next day, that is the 6th of August, 60 to 70 per cent of the populace came back.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Those who came back, were there women, children, elderly people among them?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: There were women and children, elderly people, all categories of people; however, some women and children did not come back. They went on, I don't know to which area in Croatia, possibly Crkvenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was Saborsko shelled after 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That was the beginning. After the 5th of August Saborsko was shelled every day, especially during the night.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And after -- you said that on 5th of August no damage was done to the buildings. At the later stage, were any buildings or other objects damaged?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Later, shelling was on a daily basis and many buildings were damaged, but the worst hit was the church of Saborsko because it was a tall building, it was targeted every day, and of course there was damage.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was anybody killed or injured during the shelling?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, there were some wounded among my colleagues during the shelling. It wasn't too bad, but people were very afraid. They were trying to take care of themselves, stay in shelters. But there was a lot of material damage and a lot of cattle was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In September, did you receive any help in the form of manpower, ammunition?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In September 1990 [as interpreted], yes, for a brief period, that was when I was arrested. We received assistance from Zagreb, about 100 men, around the 25th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When they arrived, were you still in the village?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was still in the village for another two or three days.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did they -- to your knowledge, did -- during the way to Saborsko, did they made any arrests?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They arrested three persons; one civilian and two persons wearing the insignia of the militia of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you see them when they brought them to the village?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. I saw them later when I was arrested myself in Plasko.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Because you managed to see them in Plaski, so how long did these people stayed in -- these arrested people stayed in Saborsko? For how long?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time when I saw them on the 25th, they had been there for two or three days.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And were they -- after they -- were they released or exchanged; do you know this?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I learned that they were exchanged for an elderly person from Sjetic Poljana [phoen]. That is a small place. I am not quite clear about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Going back to this group of 100-plus people who arrived from Zagreb, who were they? Were they soldiers? Policemen? Civilians?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: There were people, natives of Saborsko, who were mobilised in Zagreb. They had dispersed around various places in Croatia and worked there until they were mobilised, but they were originally from Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When they arrived, did you see what kinds of uniforms they wore?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw them when they arrived. They were scared. It was their first mission of that kind. I was with them on the way from Saborsko to Licka Jasenica, and they were wearing some sort of green uniform. They did not get involved into any combat at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know whether they called themselves -- or whether they had any name?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. They were called the Independent Company of Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And do you know who was their commander?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Their commander, who was it? Was it Marko Krizmanic? I don't know. The company was set up in Zagreb -- or maybe it was Luka Hodak.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What was their purpose in Saborsko? Was it just defensive or also offensive?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They were engaged in defence mostly. I don't know, in fact, what kind of equipment they had, if they had any heavy weapons or not. I don't know that. They didn't go there. They didn't come to attack; they came to defend. I'm the first to acknowledge that had we not been arrested when we were, we would have simply left. We were unable to take any more. The winter was coming. We were poorly equipped. So what I'm trying to say, they came there to defend the place but they did not succeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You -- you were arrested shortly after they arrived. But at any time between the time that Saborsko was shelled until your arrest, did you -- as policemen, did you launch any attacks against other villages, against other armed forces in that region?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't take any offensive action because we had nothing to attack with. And I have to say once again, our order was to avoid shooting if we could. And we were the happiest during those days, which were few, when we were not being attacked. And it was far from our mind to provoke any shooting ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You also -- you already mentioned that you were arrested shortly after this group from Zagreb arrived. Do you know exactly the date of your arrest?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I was arrested on the 29th of September, 1991, around 1300 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What were the circumstances of your arrest? What did you do at the time of your arrest?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I travelled through the woods towards Rakovica, a forest road called Rakovacke Uvale, in my own car.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was there anybody else with you?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Ivica Vukovic was with me. He had come from Zagreb, plus Nijaz Poric. They were the first men from Zagreb, the first mobilised men that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you wear a uniform?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was wearing a uniform and I had a side-arm and a long barrel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: On your uniform as a policeman, did you have -- did you have any patch, any insignia?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was wearing the insignia of the police right here. It was a very well-worn uniform, in tatters, but I had insignia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what kind of insignia. How did it look like?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Police. Police of the Republic of Croatia. We had the uniform of Croatian police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was there any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would that be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This is my last question, then we can break.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was there anything else on that insignia? Any picture of something?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Our uniform was a simple grey uniform with a patch that only said "Police." That's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yeah, that's it. It's a very convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we take a short break and come back at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, before we continue talking about your arrest, I have one more question relate -- in relation to the shelling. You testified earlier this morning that two JNA armoured vehicles were passing through your village almost every day or every day until the 5th of August, 1991, when the shelling started. After the shelling started, what -- what happened to these JNA armoured vehicles? Did they stop coming to your village?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After the shelling they drove again through Saborsko once more, but not again because they prevented them from driving through again. The people were up in arms, and they sort of laughed sarcastically and then they drove away towards Plitvice and never appeared again as long as I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So now I would like to return back to the end of September when you were arrested. Who arrested you?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I was ambushed while driving my car by five to six persons, one of whom was wearing a JNA uniform while others wore camouflage uniform. They were residents of Plasko. I didn't recognise the person wearing the JNA uniform, but the others I knew, and they called themselves Martic's men.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: At the time of your arrest, did you manage to notice whether these men in camouflage uniforms, whether they had any patches, any insignias?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't notice that. I didn't have time because I had my hands bound immediately. Maybe they wore some insignia, but I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Where did they take you?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They took me on foot towards the military training ground of the JNA called Tobolic, near Slunj, and after that I went to Plaski. In Tobolic their vehicles were waiting and they had come to -- on foot.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In Plaski, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I was taken first to the police outpost in Plaski, where I was detained below the staircase.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: At the police outpost, who did you see there? Were they policemen? Soldiers? Who did you see there?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: There were my colleagues there, people with whom I had worked earlier in Ogulin and in other places, plus some people I didn't know, including some wearing camouflage uniforms. But the first men I saw were my colleagues with whom I had been working just a month or two earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Those colleagues of you -- of yours, or former colleagues of yours, what kind of -- what kinds of uniform did they wear?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The same uniform, except they had a patch on the sleeve with "Militia of Krajina" written on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness document with ERN 0118-7457. I think we have little bit problem. I have a hard copy. Maybe it would be faster -- yeah. Okay. Do you have it on your screen, Your Honour? Can we place the hard copy on the ELMO and let's hope that -- yeah, on the ELMO so we all can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you have a look at the patch and tell us whether you have seen this patch.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the patch they wore on the sleeve.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: For the benefit of Judges, can you read what is written on that patch.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In Cyrillic, "Militia of Krajina."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. That's --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the -- the document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit Number 266, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So you saw this patch on uniforms of policemen in Plaski?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's the patch.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In Plaski at the police station, where were you kept?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I was detained, imprisoned in a building below the staircase which used to be a storage room, like a 2, 3 metres below the stairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How many people were there with you in that little room?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Three: I, Ivica Vukovic, and Nijaz Poric.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What did you sleep on? Did you have any blankets?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Something plastic was laid down, like a plastic mat on the floor, and everybody had the JNA-issued blanket, the grey one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you receive a meal?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In Plasko, yes, but we couldn't eat because we were beside ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How were you treated at the police station, at your captivity?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: As for treatment, of course I was expecting help from my colleagues. I asked them to release me, but Dusko Jovicic told me: Look, there is no law here. I'll try to do my best to release you or to protect you somehow, but there is no law here. That's what my colleague Dusko Jovicic told me. Because they were --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, I will interrupt you. My question was: How were you treated during your detention?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: We were beaten. I was taken to a house. They drove me around Plasko, handcuffed behind the back. They gave me to drink [as interpreted]. They shot. They made fun of us, ridiculed us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said that you were -- you were beaten. Who did the beating?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I was beaten by those groups of men dressed in camouflage uniforms, and in that group there was one man dressed in a JNA uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said "men dressed in camouflage uniforms." Did you mention that they told you who they were?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they called themselves "Marticevci," meaning Martic's men.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were -- when you were beaten, were the regular policemen present?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Regular policemen were not present, and they couldn't do anything anyway. I had already asked my former colleagues for help, but they were helpless. I could see from the general situation when somebody offered to drive me, the others would say: No, Jaksic would take him in his car. It was complete lawlessness, anarchy, and these militia groups had the main say. I don't know what they were doing there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Ms. Richterova, before you go on, there's just something -- two things which I would like to get clarified. The witness has said: "They gave me to drink," which is what is on the record. Could we have an explanation precisely what that means. And then there is another statement: "They shot." Could we please get greater clarification here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, to my question how you were treated you were, among others, answered: "They gave me to drink." What did you refer to?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They gave me beer to drink, in a tavern, while I was handcuffed behind my back. And in a coffee bar or tavern in Plasko they gave me beer to drink. I had to drink it, whether I wanted it or not. And all the time my hands were handcuffed behind my back.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you -- did you drink? Did you [sic] make you to drink?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I had no choice. They forced me. They just poured it down my throat.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you also said: "They shot." What they shot? What did they shoot at?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: While they were driving me through the centre of Plaski, in a car on the side, the -- Ljuban Korajlija was driving it, one man was driving and the other was shooting through the window while we were driving along the street, and I was in the car.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Plaski?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I stayed in Plaski about 12 days, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: After 12 days, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Then they took me to Korenica, the police station in Korenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to refer you to page 19 where you can see Titova Korenica, which is grid E3. It's the right bottom corner, and it is in the middle of that little square.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: At the police station in Korenica, who did you see there?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know anybody there. I saw policemen with the same insignia of the Krajina police and wearing uniforms, and again I saw persons in camouflage uniforms, just like in Plaski.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Talking about Plaski, do you know a person with name Nikola Madakovic?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I met that person when I was captured in Plaski. He was the first person who beat me. He beat me with a military belt, on my head.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: He came to the police station in Plaski to see me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: To your knowledge, who -- who he was?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: He was later the president of the municipality. He was a local leader in the Republic of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now, returning to Korenica. In Korenica you -- you were taken at the police station. Where in the police station, where were you kept?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: There were three detention cells there, and I was in cell number 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were there some other people detained together with you?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In my cell, cell number 3, there was Nikola Pemper and Ignjac Ivanus. They were from Otocac, from Gospic. Ignjac Ivanus came from the Croatian Zagorje region and he was a police station commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: These two other men, were they of Croat ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, both Nikola and Ignjac were of Croatian ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you able to see whether there were other people detained in other cells?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't able to see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Who was in charge in Korenica?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know that. We were in cells, so we don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And how were you treated in Korenica at that police station?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In the police station in Korenica, when I got there I was handcuffed. My hands were handcuffed behind my back. I was put in the cell like that, and the handcuffs were taken off only on the following day. The way they handcuffed me in Plaski, that's how I was left in Korenica. Apparently they couldn't find the key. Nikola Pemper gave me water to drink.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You were beaten in -- at Plaski police station. What about at Korenica police station?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I was beaten even more badly there and my face was cut with a knife.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges who did the beatings?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the person. That person was naked to the waist and was carrying a knife and had a black rag around his head. This was in the Korenica police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you were beaten, were the other policemen present?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but they behaved as if nothing was happening. They were sitting on the other side, drinking something, beer or coffee or whatever. It was in the same room where he was beating me, and they were just sitting there and they were completely indifferent.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How long did you stay? Approximately how long did you stay at Korenica police station?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but I think about ten days. It was a cell, solitary confinement. I could see when it was day-light, but I can't tell you the exact number of days, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You mentioned this beating. Were you -- was this the only occasion when you were beaten or were there more than one occasion when you were beaten?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I was beaten more than once but this was the worst time. In the evening, when the pubs in Korenica closed, they would come to beat people, to punch people or to kick them in the head. But the worst thing that happened to me when I was cut with a knife.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And whenever you were beaten, were the policemen with the sign Militia Krajina, were they always present?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were present but they didn't react. It was as if they weren't there. I would look at them and they would not respond in any way. In Plasko they tried but couldn't, because in Plasko we were acquaintances, and here they didn't even try.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said that you stayed here for about ten days. Where did you go after this time?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Then a JNA vehicle came to fetch us, 110, that's an all-terrain vehicle. It was referred to as the "110." And we were taken to the Zeljava military airport in Bihac. That's on the border between Croatia and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And at this airport, for how long were you -- how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I think I stayed there -- it was in a warehouse. There were several of us there, and I was there until the end of October, maybe eight days, and then I was taken to Manjaca in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said that it was a military airport. Was it the JNA who was in charge at that airport?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was a JNA military airport and there were persons in blue JNA uniforms there. It was a military airport, and they had blue uniforms. There were also those in olive-green uniforms. There were conscripts there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: These men in blue uniforms, do you remember whether they wore any belts?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That was the military police, and they wore white belts. Those belonged to the military police of the then-JNA. Sometimes they would wear green uniforms. It was unclear to me, because they would change uniforms, but they were JNA uniforms. And there were groups of men there whom I didn't know what they were and they wore camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you beaten at this detention facility?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We slept in a warehouse at Palace and they beat us there. They beat Nikola Pemper worst, and then me. I don't know why they beat Nikola Pemper so badly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Again, who did the beating?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Persons with white belts. One day they would be wearing a green JNA uniform, the next day a blue uniform. And then a military policeman said to me that those were our colleagues from Zagreb. There were five of them. They had left the Republic of Croatia and the Ministry of the Interior and gone to the Zeljava airport. A military policeman said: It's your colleagues who are beating you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And finally, you mentioned you were taken to Manjaca. Can you tell the Judges where Manjaca is.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Manjaca is in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know which is the biggest town near to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The biggest town near Manjaca is Banja Luka. There was a military training ground there and the JNA barracks. In Manjaca, that is. And it's just above Banja Luka. Banja Luka is the biggest town there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did I understand correctly that Manjaca was this military training ground?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were barracks there, hangars. We were locked up in hangars where they kept cattle.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How many people were there together with you? How many people were there detained?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: There were three hangars in all, and I think about 200 men. I was in the third one. There were wounded men there. The policemen from Kostajnica who had been captured before me, they were up there. There were about 200 men. I know that because when the exchange was carried out, then I learned how many of us there were. I couldn't know at the time how many men were imprisoned in those three hangars.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know which ethnicity were these people who were detained in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know that. I know it was policemen from Hrvatska Kostajnica, but whether there were also people of other ethnicities, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: At any time during your detention, either in Plaski, Korenica, Bihac, or Manjaca, were you taken -- were you told why you had been arrested or why were you detained?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. We never got a specific reply. They would just say vulgar words and say that the Republic of Croatia would cost us dearly. They would say nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were exchanged. When was it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: We were exchanged at the border between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia in Slavonski and Bosanski Samac on the bridge on the 9th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And after you were exchanged, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: To Zagreb, for treatment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: At --

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Bjelovar and then Zagreb, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: After your exchange in 1991, did you go at any time back to Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The first time I returned to Saborsko was during Operation Storm on the 6th or 7th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you came to Saborsko in 1995, how did the village look like?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't recognise it. It didn't exist. You could see just the bushes. It was all overgrown and the road was overgrown. It was all covered with bushes. There was nothing there. It was a ghost place, just thorns and bushes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The houses, were they all destroyed or were there some which stay intact?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It's not just that they were damaged; they didn't exist. I didn't see a single house. I only recognised the church. It was a heap of rubble. Because the church had been a big building, so I recognised that heap of rubble as the church. But as for the rest, you couldn't tell where the houses had been. I recognised just the church and the school because there were heaps of stones there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you visit some other villages in that region?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't because I was assigned to Plaski-Saborsko and I didn't have time to go around and look at other places. It was only later on, but for the first month or two, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You say "only later on," so later on did you visit some other villages?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, later on, as I said, I visited Plitvice, and that was it. And Rakovica, later on, but in the first month I didn't go anywhere. I was on the Saborsko-Ogulin route.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You visited Rakovica. Rakovica, was it a Serb village or a Croat village?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It was a Croat village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And how did you find it? How did Rakovica look like?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It was partially destroyed. Half of it was destroyed. It was all neglected but it didn't look like Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In Saborsko in 1995, did you participate in exhumations?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was personally present. The first exhumations began on the 18th of October, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell us, was there just one site or were there more than one site where you found dead people?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In Saborsko there was several sites, several exhumations and several mass graves. The biggest was in Popov Sanac, where 14 bodies were found.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges approximately how many people were exhumed in Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In Saborsko, 20-something people were exhumed and seven are still missing. Some were in Popov Sanac, which was the biggest mass grave, some were in Borik, and there were also people who were burned in their houses. Those were the sick, the elderly. They found skeletons in the houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know --

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Not in the houses, but at the hearths.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know approximately how old these people were, those who you found? Who was the oldest and who was the youngest?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The age was 70, 80, 65. There were two elderly people who were 100 years old. Those two people were 100 years old. They were found, one in Popov Sanac, in the mass grave there, and the other one in Srjeni [phoen]. The youngest was a sick woman. I think she was born in 1960. It was a sick female, and she was found burned alive on her bed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You mentioned this one woman. Were there more than one woman who was exhumed?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I told you who the youngest was and who the oldest were. And the other women I mentioned were about 70.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vukovic. I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Richterova. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, my name is Predrag Milovancevic. I am Defence counsel for Milan Martic. This stage of your examination is called cross-examination. I will put questions to you, and you will respond in the way you know. As we understand each other, for the sake of the interpreters, please let's make a pause between question and answer. In your statement which you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor, you said that until 1989 you worked in the Plitvice Lakes National Park. Can you tell us what sort of work you did.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I was in the building construction department, and we put together wooden houses all over the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could one say that you were employed in a company called Plitvice Lakes National Park?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The name of the company Plitvice Lakes National Park mentions the lakes that make up the national park. Do you know how many employees there were in that company? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I think it was about a thousand people in all the various departments. It was a huge company. It was over a thousand people who were employed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor you said that in 1989 you and several others at one point felt unwanted in the area where the Serbs were in the majority, that you felt uncomfortable, and that you decided to leave although nothing specific happened. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There was a group of people who would sing Chetnik songs in the evenings. There were provocations. People would jeer at us. We went to our boss; he didn't say anything. Because we had gone to have a meal, not to listen to people singing Chetnik songs. It would happen in the evenings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, all that was going on in a restaurant and the staff were singing songs?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, patrons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the OTP you said that in 1989 because of that situation, because of the feeling that you were unwelcome in areas where Serbs were a majority, you left your job and went to Saborsko where your parents lived and remained there until 1990 when you found a job with the police force.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Also in your statement you said that in Saborsko there was a population of about 800 and only a few Serbs. Was that the population?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Around 800 residents in total, and only about four Serb houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement we read when you described your stay in Saborsko while you were unemployed, that is, until the end of 1990, that you felt that the situation was changing, although there were no particular incidents in Saborsko. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Things were happening all around, although not in Saborsko. But things were happening all over the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You stated that you had left Plitvice because you felt unwelcome in a place where Serbs were a majority and you went to Saborsko which had a majority Croat population. And again you felt something was going on. Was something really going on or was it all within you?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Democracy was being introduced, things were really happening. The state of Croatia was coming into being.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that this onset of democracy and the creation of the Republic of Croatia was the source of your feeling of unease?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No; on the contrary. I was glad that we had democracy and freedom of speech and thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was this freedom given to everyone or only to some?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: To everyone. The word "democracy" is clear; we all know what its meaning is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement describing year 1990 in Saborsko, you said there were no political activities in that place; however, you also stated that in end-March -- in end-February or perhaps March 1990 one rally was held, and another one in July, and that later yet another rally was held with the participation of Jovan Opacic. Can you tell me who organised the rallies in February/March and in July, and what kind of rallies were they?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Those were rallies as part of the electoral campaign in March and in July. That's when the elections were being held. Those were political rallies. Democracy had come and rallies could be organised. There were no bans, no communism anymore. Rallies were being held by all the new political parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what political parties organised these two rallies?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. It was the Croatian Democratic Union, HDZ. And there were more rallies. Those were not the only ones. Other political parties also had their rallies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about the rallies held in Saborsko or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In Saborsko, there were many public debates and rallies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the topic of those public debates? It was election time and what was discussed?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Democracy. New winds were blowing and the state of Croatia was coming into being, whereas the state of Yugoslavia was falling apart. It wasn't happening only in our country. The Berlin Wall was coming down, Czechoslovakia was breaking up. It was the onset of democracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was the main purpose, main goal, of the HDZ to create an independent state of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Not only of the HDZ. There were a number of parties at the time who had that as a goal. There was no more communism, no more diktat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that in the first half of 1991, elections were held for the first time in Croatia. Do you mean to say the first multi-party elections won by the HDZ that won a two-third majority in the parliament of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I mean the first democratic multi-party elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the organisation of key political parties in Croatia that were working for an independent state, amendments were introduced to the Croatian constitution whereby the Serbs, who had until then been a constituent nation, were to become a national minority?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I think the Serbs were not a national minority in the first Croatian institution -- constitution because there were more than 11 per cent of them in the total population. The Serbs were not a national minority according to the constitution, because it was adopted in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In that year, 1990, do you know if the Serbs tried to present their demands for autonomy?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Not that I know of. I don't know what that means "autonomy." If you have all your rights protected by the constitution, what more is there to seek? They were not even a minority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said you heard it being said that in August 1990 some barricades were being put up but not in Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said in your statement to the OTP that in August 1990 barricades were being put up in Serb-held areas of Croatia, according to what you heard.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, barricades already existed at that time, but not in Saborsko. It was all over the media and it is documented. Let us just remember that tourist season and how it developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying that the barricades were put up in August 1990? You said yourself it was the tourist season.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's as accurately as I can put it. I don't know if it was August or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what was the immediate cause for putting up barricades? Do you know that the Croatian government banned a referendum of the Serbs in Croatia concerning their autonomy?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I talked to many Serbs, and I never heard of that. And to date we still don't know why it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said in your statement that after the May referendum a significant number of Serbs from other villages stopped coming to Saborsko; however, you specified that that May referendum happened in 1990. My question is: Was it actually in 1991, after the first multi-party elections?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it must have been a slip on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was the question asked at that May referendum in Croatia in 1991 for the whole population of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: What? What?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What did the people vote about at that referendum in May 1991? Was that decision about the independence of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was about the Independent State of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that all residents of Saborsko voted for the HDZ at the first multi-party elections, and you said that all political parties in Croatia were in favour of an independent Croatian state. You also said that after the May referendum in 1991 the Serbs from the surrounding villages stopped coming to Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Not all Serbs. Some of them. Not all of them. I never speak in such general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know why some Serbs from the surrounding villages stopped coming to Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it became clear from the result, from all that we saw later: The Serbs who stopped coming were those who were dreaming of Greater Serbia, with the borders Karlovac, Virovitica, Karlobag. We saw the creation of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and the goal expressed in the memorandum coming from Belgrade that all Serbs should live in one state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We will come back to that topic. Let us go back to the chronological order of events. You said that in 1990 you became unemployed. By the end of the year you found a job with the police of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 15th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At the time when you found that job in the police of the Republic of Croatia, had you finished some sort of police school?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: First I was approved by the medical panel - you know the procedure - and then I got the job. After that, I attended training courses, workshops, seminars, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So before that job in the police, you did not have any training to be a policeman; you got it only later?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I had some education. This was just retraining. I had graduated from a high school, and the training I got was just retraining.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That training course, was it in Zagreb, in Simunska Street?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, it was called education seminars and advanced training, in Ogulin and in Karlovac. We had theoretical and practical training, alternating. We learned about the law on criminal procedure, the criminal code, the law on the police force, et cetera. Our group had 20 persons in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you found that employment in December 1990, with which police station was it, in Ogulin or in Karlovac?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The police station was in Ogulin, but it belonged to the police administration of Karlovac. You have the Ministry of Interior at the top of the pyramid; below it, you have police administrations; and the level below are police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Among the 20 persons who were employed together with you, were there any men who had been policemen prior to that, who had graduated already from police schools?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the HDZ had any say in the selection of trainees, cadets, for that police corps?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. But I know why you're asking. Even Serbs were admitted at that time. Damir Vorkapic and another man, a Serb, were in my group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that after being admitted to the police force and after your training in Ogulin you worked as a regular policeman and got training on the job. How long did that last?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: From December until Easter, the end of March, actually, 1991. Immediately after getting a contract, we started the training.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of uniforms were worn by the police that belonged to the MUP of Croatia at the time?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Normal uniforms, and I had normal insignia. The patch on the sleeve said "militia" which was the former name for the police in Yugoslavia. It hadn't yet changed to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1990, while the former Yugoslavia still existed, the sleeve patch said "Milicija" and a five-pointed star on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When did the new police force of Croatia come into being?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't called "Milicija" anymore. It became "Policija," police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was it with a chequer-board flag?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It's not the chequer-board emblem. It's the historic Croatian coat of arms, and the five-pointed star was replaced by the -- that historic Croatian coat of arms in January 1991. I absolutely reject the term "chequer-board" flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At that time were all members of the police asked to sign a declaration of loyalty to the government of the Republic of Croatia in 1991?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Those who were already in the police remained in the police. We who were new took an oath, as happens in every system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say that on the 1st of April, 1991, you were deployed as a policeman in Saborsko. Had there been a police substation in Saborsko until then?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, it was the first time it was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was Marko Vukovic also deployed there as a policeman, together with you?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the police substation in Saborsko had about 20 active-duty policemen. Your colleague said there were 26 or 28, plus four to five reserve policemen; a total of 32.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the approximate number. There were about ten reservists and 20-plus active-duty policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could one say then that the number of policemen in Saborsko in the police outpost was 32?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't believe that. A lot of time has elapsed, but there are lists. I don't want to give you any numbers off the top of my head. You can look it up in the records, the records of the payroll. I cannot give you precise numbers; it was 15 or 16 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that all the policemen had automatic rifles and that the active-duty policemen also had side-arms, pistols.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, pistols, side-arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When the Serb police outpost was established in Saborsko on the 1st of April, 1991, you linked its establishment to what you called the epicentre of evil, referring to the events in Plitvice on the 1st of April, 1991. Are you referring to the events that happened on the Catholic Easter 1991?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to confuse the Catholic Easter with the first incident that occurred at Plitvice. Catholic Easter is celebrated all over the world. What has it got to do with the Plitvice Lakes? It just happened to coincide. What has it got to do with Easter?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you because there is information that the Catholic Easter took place on the 31st of March, 1991, and the 1st of April is the next day. So is that what you're referring to when you refer to the epicentre of evil?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I know what happened at Plitvice on the 1st of April, 1991; it has nothing to do with the Catholic holiday of Easter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on Catholic Easter the Croatian police carried out an armed attack on Plitvice?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That's not correct. Who attacked whom, everybody knows that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were you at Plitvice at the time?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was in Ogulin. I arrived in Saborsko in the late afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were you in command of units of the Croatian police at Plitvice on that day when there was a clash?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I became a commander only in 1995, during Operation Storm. Up to that time, I was not a commander; as I said, I was the operations duty officer. My command duties began during Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If that's correct, then how do you know what happened at Plitvice and who attacked whom?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course I know; it was nearby. What kind of policeman would I be if I didn't know what was happening at Plitvice?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On that day at Plitvice when there was an armed conflict, were two men killed?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if anybody was killed?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I know that one was killed; that's what I learned in the media, because I wasn't actually there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And that one person who was killed, what ethnicity was he, do you know?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: He was a Croatian policeman, an employee of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And you don't know that a Serb was killed on that day?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. In what capacity was he killed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is anyone's capacity a reason not to consider a person a victim if he's a victim?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what this was about, and I don't know who was killed and in what capacity. As I say, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that pursuant to a decision by the Presidency of the country, the JNA intervened at Plitvice and prevent an escalation of the conflict on the 1st of April, 1991, or the evening of the 31st of March, 1991?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The JNA did not prevent the conflict; it fanned the flames. That was the problem, because to arrive in tanks into a national park against some 20 policemen ... They damaged the water barriers, and the ecological association and the greens are still dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In 1991 were the Plitvice Lakes part of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, they were in Croatia that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was Croatia in April or the 31st of March still in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. The elections had been held a year before, the multi-party elections, and democracy was already in force and the Croatian state had already been created.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you wish to say that your understanding of Croatian democracy meant that the federal state no longer existed, that Yugoslavia no longer existed, and that the JNA had no right to intervene there?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot give you an answer to those questions. I don't know why one should fear democracy anywhere in the world, the right of people to think, to speak. Otherwise, where there is no democracy we would only have diktat, like the one we had for 40 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When the police station was established in Saborsko, substation, you said there was some 30 policemen there of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia. Where were they deployed and what duties did they perform?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Regular daily police work, that's what they did. Check-points, beat duty, patrol duty, keeping public law and order, providing public security.
